title: Thinking Like a Programmer
sub: Decompose problems, pick the right algorithm and data structure, debug on purpose and keep history with git
goals: Break a vague task into steps and write it as pseudocode or an ASCII flowchart
Explain linear versus binary search and what O(n) and O(log n) mean, with measurements
Choose between a list, dictionary, set, stack, queue, tree and graph for a networking task
Debug with the loop reproduce, isolate, hypothesize, test, and read an error message from the bottom up
Track your work in a git repository with branches, merges and a remote
Edit a file with nano and get out of vim alive

blocks.text: Everything in the rest of this book, every pipeline, shell script and Python tool, is the same activity: turning a question into steps a machine can follow, then finding out why it does not do what you expected. That skill is separate from any language. In this chapter you will learn how a program is built, how to break a task apart, the handful of algorithms and data structures that account for most real code, a debugging method you can apply to anything, and git, the tool that lets you break things freely because you can always go back.
Most sections end with something to type. Make a folder for this chapter's experiments: `mkdir -p ~/lab/think && cd ~/lab/think`. The git sections use a repository you will create there.
How a program gets built

A **program** is a list of instructions plus the data they work on. Every program, from `ls` to a web browser, has the same outline: take **input**, **process** it, produce **output**. A pipeline such as `cat access.log | grep 404 | wc -l` is exactly that, three times in a row.
You write instructions as **source code**, in text a human can read. The CPU only understands machine code, so something must translate. There are two common routes:

blocks.code:
compiled (C, Rust, Go)                            interpreted (zsh, Python)

 ⟪c:source⟫ ──▶ ⟪y:compiler⟫ ──▶ ⟪g:machine code file⟫ ──▶ CPU      ⟪c:source⟫ ──▶ ⟪y:interpreter⟫ ──▶ CPU
   once, ahead of time        run many times             read and executed line by line, every run

blocks.text: A compiled program is translated once into a file of machine code (`ls` is one). An interpreted program is read by another program, the interpreter (`zsh`, `python3`), each time you run it. Interpreted languages start instantly and are easy to change, which is why this book uses them. The trade-off is raw speed, which rarely matters for the tasks here.

The part you control is the **source text**: its logic is the same whichever route it takes. When you type `python3 tool.py`, the shell starts `python3` as a process, hands it the file name as an argument, and the interpreter reads the file, executes it, and exits with a status code the shell stores in `$?` (see [Streams, Redirection & Pipes](#pipes)).
Decomposing a problem

Beginners stall because they stare at the whole problem. Professionals do **top-down decomposition**: write the goal as one sentence, split it into 3 to 5 sub-goals, and split each until a step is something you could type in one line.
Take "tell me whether my internet connection is working". That is vague. Decompose it by the layers you met in [Computer networks](#networks):

items.text: Is my interface up and does it have an IP address? (`ifconfig`)
Can I reach my router? (`ping` the gateway)
Can I reach something beyond it by IP? (`ping 1.1.1.1`)
Can I turn a name into an address? (`dig example.com`)
Can I fetch a web page? (`curl`)

blocks.text: Each step is now small, testable on its own and independent enough to run in a different order. That list is the design of `netcheck.zsh`, which you build in [Scripting](#scripting). Notice that the decomposition also tells you how to *diagnose*: the first failing step is where to look.
Pseudocode

**Pseudocode** is the plan written in plain English with the shape of code: sequence, decisions, loops. It has no syntax rules, so you cannot get it wrong, and you can check the logic before fighting a language.

Every construct here exists in every language you will use: a **variable** (`failures`), a **loop** (`for each`), a **decision** (`if`/`else`), and an **action** that talks to the outside world (`ping`, `print`, `exit`).
Flowcharts in ASCII
A flowchart shows the same logic as boxes and arrows, which helps when there are many branches. Diamonds are decisions.

blocks.title: Make the first version stupidly small

blocks.text: Build the smallest thing that gives you one real answer, run it, then grow it. A script that pings one host and prints `up` or `down` is a working program. A script that does everything and has never run is a pile of guesses.
Decomposition in a pipeline

The same method works on the shell. The question "which client made the most requests?" decomposes into stages, and you check each before adding the next. This is the method from [Streams, Redirection & Pipes](#pipes) applied deliberately:

Stage by stage: extract the IP column, group identical IPs, count each group, rank the counts, keep one. If the final answer looked wrong, you would know which stage to test, because you tested them in order.
The building blocks every language shares
Whatever the syntax, a program is made of the same five ideas. If you recognize them, a new language is just new spelling.

blocks.text: A **type** matters because it decides what operations make sense: you can add two numbers, join two strings, but `"80" + 1` is an error in Python because one side is text. Most beginner bugs come from a value being a different type than you thought, such as a port number read from a file, which is always text until you convert it.

A **function** is the most important tool for managing complexity. It gives a name to a step (`is_private(ip)`), so the rest of the program reads like the pseudocode. The inputs are **parameters**, the output is the **return value**, and variables created inside are **local**: they vanish when the function ends and cannot clobber the rest of the program.

blocks.text: That is the whole vocabulary: variables hold state, decisions choose a path, loops repeat, functions name things. The rest of programming is combining them well.
Trace tables: be the computer

When code misbehaves, stop guessing and **execute it by hand**. A trace table has one row per step and one column per variable. Fill it in exactly as the computer would, and the bug usually appears as the row where your expectation and the table disagree.

blocks.code:
total = 0
for n in [3, 5, 2]:
    total = total + n
    print(f"n={n} total={total}")
print("final", total)
blocks.out:
n=3 total=3
n=5 total=8
n=2 total=10
final 10

Doing this on paper for ten lines is slow, which is the point: it forces you to read what the code *says* rather than what you meant.
Algorithms with intuition

An **algorithm** is a precise procedure for solving a class of problem. You already use them: `sort` implements one, `grep` another. Two ideas let you reason about any algorithm: what it does, and how its cost grows with the size of the input.
Searching: linear versus binary
**Linear search** checks items one by one from the start until it finds the target. If the list has `n` items, you may need up to `n` checks.

**Binary search** requires a **sorted** list. Look at the middle item. If it is the target, done. If the target is smaller, discard the upper half; if larger, discard the lower half. Repeat on what is left. Each step halves the search space.
Count the work rather than trusting a story. This program counts how many items each method looks at when the target is the last element:

A million items cost the linear search a million looks and the binary search about twenty. That gap is why databases keep indexes sorted, why `git bisect` finds a bad commit among thousands in a dozen steps, and why you sort before you search.
Sorting

Sorting puts items in order, which makes searching, deduplicating (`uniq`) and merging (`comm`, `join`) possible. The simplest algorithm, **selection sort**, repeatedly finds the smallest remaining item and swaps it to the front:

blocks.code:
data = [5, 2, 9, 1]
for i in range(len(data) - 1):
    smallest = min(range(i, len(data)), key=lambda j: data[j])
    data[i], data[smallest] = data[smallest], data[i]
    print(f"pass {i + 1}: {data}")

blocks.text: It does about `n * n / 2` comparisons, which is fine for 4 items and painful for a million. Real systems use algorithms like merge sort and Timsort (what Python's `sorted()` uses) that need about `n * log n` steps. You will almost never write a sort yourself; you will choose the right key and know that `sorted()` is **stable**: equal items keep their original order. The shell's `sort` is not stable by default (it breaks ties by comparing whole lines) until you add `-s`, which is what makes `sort -k2 | sort -s -k1` style tricks work.
Complexity: how cost grows
**Big-O notation** describes how an algorithm's work grows as `n` grows, ignoring constant factors. It lets you predict whether something will still be fast when the input is 1000 times larger.

blocks.text: At a million items, `n²` is a trillion operations, hours of work, while `n log n` is about twenty million, a fraction of a second. When a script is mysteriously slow on big input, look for a loop inside a loop over the same data.
Measure rather than guess. This block times a membership test in a list (O(n): a scan) against a set (O(1): a hash lookup). The numbers differ on every machine, so run it and read your own result:

blocks.code:
import timeit
n = 100_000
as_list = list(range(n))
as_set = set(as_list)
target = n - 1
t_list = timeit.timeit(lambda: target in as_list, number=200)
t_set = timeit.timeit(lambda: target in as_set, number=200)
print(f"list: {t_list * 1000:.2f} ms   set: {t_set * 1000:.4f} ms   ratio: {t_list / t_set:,.0f}x")

blocks.text: The ratio is typically in the thousands. Choosing the right container, the next topic, is often a bigger win than any clever code.
Data structures and where networking uses them
A **data structure** is a way of organizing data so the operations you need are cheap. The choice usually matters more than the algorithm.

Idea
Fast at
Networking example
rows: lines of a log, hops of a traceroute
ARP table (IP to MAC), routing cache, requests per IP
the set of blocked IPs, hosts seen so far

blocks.text: The next program touches four of them: a dictionary as an ARP table, a set to remove duplicates, a queue to search a graph level by level (**breadth-first search**, which finds the path with the fewest hops), and a tree built from nested dictionaries.

The graph is what routers are solving: find a good path through a web of links. The tree is how DNS organizes names, and why `www.example.com` is resolved right to left. You will use dictionaries and sets constantly in Python, covered properly in [Python data structures](#py-data).
Debugging as a method
Code that works the first time is luck. Debugging is the normal state of programming, and it goes much faster as a method than as flailing. The method is the same as in any experiment:

items.text: **Reproduce.** Find the smallest input and the exact steps that make the bug appear every time. If you cannot make it happen on demand, you cannot know when it is fixed.
**Isolate.** Shrink the problem. Cut the pipeline at each `|`. Comment out half the script. Replace real data with three lines. Keep halving (binary search again) until the bug lives in a few lines.
**Hypothesize.** Say out loud what you think is wrong: "I think the second `sort` is missing, so `uniq` sees duplicates that are not adjacent." A hypothesis must predict something you can check.
**Test.** Run the experiment that would prove the hypothesis wrong. Change **one** thing at a time. If the result matches, fix it; if not, discard the hypothesis and form another.

blocks.text: If you change several things and the bug disappears, you do not know which change fixed it, or whether you hid the bug. One change, one run.
Read the error message, bottom first

Error messages are the most useful clue you will ever get and the most commonly skipped. In Python, read a traceback from the **bottom**: the last line is the exception type and message; the lines above are the chain of calls that led there, with file names and line numbers.

blocks.code:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "ports.py", line 9, in <module>
    print(expand("80,443,8000-8003"))
  File "ports.py", line 5, in expand
    lo, hi = part.split("-")
ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 2, got 1)

blocks.text: Bottom line: a `ValueError`, "expected 2, got 1" while unpacking. The line above shows the code: `part.split("-")` returned one piece, because the part `80` has no dash. The bug is that the code assumes every part is a range. Total time to understand: ten seconds, because you read the message.

Shell errors work the same way. `zsh: command not found: pnig` is a typo, `Permission denied` is the execute bit or ownership, `No such file or directory` is a wrong path or a wrong working directory. When a message uses words you do not know, search for the **exact text**, minus your own file names.
This block fails on purpose so you can read the error yourself, then fix it:

The first call prints `6.0`. The second raises `ZeroDivisionError: division by zero` because an empty list has length 0. Decide what an empty list should mean (return 0? raise a clearer error?) and handle it explicitly.
Print debugging and the rubber duck

The cheapest debugger is output. Print the values you assume: the variable before the failing line, the length of the list, the type. In the shell use `echo`, `set -x` (`setopt xtrace` in zsh, covered in [Scripting](#scripting)) or put `tee debug.txt` between pipeline stages. In Python, `print(repr(value), type(value))` shows exactly what you have, including invisible whitespace. Remove the prints when done.

**Rubber duck debugging** is explaining the code, line by line, to someone who knows nothing, even a rubber duck. You find the bug mid-sentence about half the time, because explaining forces you to state your assumptions, and a wrong assumption is the bug.
Where bugs live
Most bugs fall into a few families. Check them first:

items.text: **Off by one.** A loop one step short or long, a slice that drops the last item. Test the first item, the last item and an empty input.
**Wrong type.** Text where you expected a number (`"80"` versus `80`), or a string with a trailing newline.
**Wrong assumption about the data.** The log has a line with a different shape; the file has Windows line endings; a field contains a space.
**State you forgot.** A variable still holds the value from the previous iteration, or the shell's current directory is not what you think.
**The environment.** The command you ran is a different version or a different program than you assumed (BSD versus GNU flags on macOS), or `PATH` finds something else.

blocks.text: The same method on a network problem

Reproduce, isolate, hypothesize and test apply unchanged to "the internet is down". The network is a stack of layers, so isolating means halving the stack: if you can ping your gateway, the cable or Wi-Fi link and your IP configuration work, and the fault is further out. If you can ping `1.1.1.1` but cannot resolve names, the fault is DNS. The flowchart below encodes that halving. Click through it with a real or imagined symptom, and note that every box asks a question one command can answer. [Troubleshooting a network](#troubleshoot) later builds the commands behind each box.
Version control with git

**Version control** records the history of your files so you can compare, undo and branch. **Git** is the universal tool, and it is already on your Mac with the Xcode command line tools (check with `git --version`). It turns a folder into a **repository**: your files plus a hidden `.git` directory holding every saved version.
Git has three places a change can be, and most commands move changes between them:

blocks.code:
⟪c:working tree⟫               ⟪y:staging area (index)⟫           ⟪g:repository (history)⟫
  the files you edit            what the next commit will contain    commits, forever

       │   git add file ───────────▶ │                                    │
       │                             │   git commit ────────────────────▶ │
       │ ◀──────────────── git restore --staged                           │
       │ ◀───────────────────────────────────────── git restore file      │

blocks.text: A **commit** is a snapshot of the staged files with a message, an author and a pointer to the previous commit. A **branch** is only a movable label pointing at a commit, so creating one is instant. `HEAD` is the label for "where you are now".

blocks.code:
main:           ● ── ● ── ● ── ● ── ● ── ◉ main
                              \          /
  feature:                     ● ── ● ── ●        merge brings the branch back into main

blocks.text: Tell git who you are once. These values go into every commit you make:

blocks.code:
git config --global user.name "{{name}}"
git config --global user.email "{{email}}"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main

blocks.name: git init
blocks.sum: Turn the current folder into a git repository.

how.text: `git init` creates a `.git` directory in the current folder (or in `directory`) holding the object database, branch pointers and configuration. It does not record any files yet; the folder is an empty repository until you add and commit. `-b main` names the first branch, which avoids the old default of `master` if you have not set `init.defaultBranch`.

flags.d: Name the initial branch.
Create a repository with no working tree, used as a shared remote.

examples.desc: Start a repository for a script
Find every git repository under your lab folder

gotchas: Never run `git init` in your home folder. Git would watch every file you own. If it happens, delete the stray `~/.git` directory.

blocks.name: git status
blocks.sum: Show which files are modified, staged, untracked or in conflict.

how.text: `git status` compares three things: the working tree, the staging area and the last commit. It lists changes staged for commit, changes not yet staged, and untracked files, and it suggests the command to move each. Run it constantly: it is read-only and tells you exactly where you are. `-s` prints a compact two-column form where the left letter is the staged state and the right letter the working-tree state (`M` modified, `A` added, `??` untracked, `UU` conflict).

flags.d: Short, one line per file.
Include the branch name in short output.

examples.desc: Short status
List only the names of modified files
Count untracked files

gotchas: A file that git already tracks stays tracked after you add it to `.gitignore`. Stop tracking it with `git rm --cached file`.

blocks.name: git add
blocks.sum: Stage changes so that the next commit includes them.

how.text: Git commits exactly what is in the staging area, so `git add` selects which changes go into the next snapshot. That lets you make one logical commit out of a messy working tree. `git add file` stages the file's current contents; if you edit the file again afterwards, the new edits are not staged. `-p` walks you through each changed hunk and asks yes or no.

flags.d: Interactively choose which hunks to stage.
Stage all changes, including deletions, everywhere in the repository.

examples.desc: Stage one file
Stage everything that is not ignored
Stage every modified tracked file, but not new ones
examples.code: git status -s | awk '$1 == "M" {print $2}' | xargs git add

gotchas: `git add .` stages everything below the current directory, including files you did not mean to commit. Run `git status` first, and put secrets and build output in `.gitignore`.

blocks.name: git commit
blocks.sum: Record the staged changes as a new commit with a message.

how.text: A commit stores a snapshot of the staging area, plus your name, the time, the message and the parent commit. Each commit is identified by a 40-character hash (the first 7 usually suffice). Without `-m`, git opens your editor for the message: configure it with `git config --global core.editor nano` if you do not want vim. Write the first line as an instruction under about 50 characters ("Add retry loop"); it is what `git log --oneline` shows.

flags.d: Use this message instead of opening the editor.
Automatically stage changes to files git already tracks.
Replace the last commit with a new one (fix the message or add a forgotten file). Do not amend commits you have already pushed.

examples.out:
[main 3d1f717] Add check.zsh
 1 file changed, 8 insertions(+)

examples.desc: Commit all tracked changes with a dated message

gotchas: If git says `Author identity unknown`, you skipped `git config --global user.name` and `user.email`.

how.text: `git log` walks backwards from `HEAD` along parent pointers and prints each commit. The default output is long, so you will usually add `--oneline` (hash and subject). `--graph --decorate --all` draws the branch structure with branch names, which is the best way to see what a merge did. Adding a path after `--` restricts the history to commits that touched that file. Output goes through a pager: press `q` to leave it.

Draw the commit graph in ASCII.
Include all branches, not just the current one.
Show only the last N commits.
Show which files each commit changed.

* 3d1f717 Add check.zsh

blocks.name: git diff
blocks.sum: Show exactly which lines changed between two states.

how.text: With no arguments `git diff` compares the working tree to the staging area: what you changed but have not yet staged. `--staged` compares the staging area to the last commit: what the next commit will contain. Lines starting with `-` are removed, `+` are added, and `@@` lines give the position. Read the diff before every commit; it is the best way to catch stray debug prints.

flags.d: Compare staged changes to the last commit.
Print only the names of changed files.
Summarize changes per file.

examples.desc: Review what you are about to commit
Count lines in every changed file

how.text: A branch is a pointer to a commit, so `git branch name` costs almost nothing. With no arguments it lists local branches and marks the current one with `*`. `-vv` also shows the last commit and the upstream branch it tracks. `-d` deletes a branch that is already merged; `-D` forces deletion. Deleting a branch deletes only the label, and the commits remain reachable by hash for a while.

flags.d: List local and remote-tracking branches.
Show last commit and upstream for each branch.
Delete a merged branch.

examples.out:

* main            469c041 [origin/main] Add notes

examples.desc: Delete all merged branches except main
examples.code: git branch --merged | grep -v '^\*' | grep -v main | xargs -n 1 git branch -d

blocks.name: git switch
blocks.sum: Move to another branch, or create and move to a new one.

how.text: `git switch` changes `HEAD` to another branch and rewrites your working tree to match that branch's last commit. `-c` creates the branch from where you are and switches in one step. Git refuses to switch if you have uncommitted changes that would be overwritten; commit them, or park them with `git stash`. `git switch -` returns to the previous branch. (`git checkout` still works for the same purpose and is what older tutorials show.)

flags.d: Create the branch and switch to it.
Switch back to the previously checked-out branch.

examples.desc: Start a feature branch
Switch to the most recently committed branch
examples.code: git for-each-ref --sort=-committerdate --format='%(refname:short)' refs/heads | head -1 | xargs git switch

blocks.name: git merge
blocks.sum: Bring the commits of another branch into the current one.

how.text: `git merge branch` finds the common ancestor of the two branches and combines the changes made on each side. If the current branch has not moved since the other branch split off, git simply moves the pointer forward (a **fast-forward**). Otherwise it creates a **merge commit** with two parents. If both sides changed the same lines, git stops with a **conflict** and marks the file for you to resolve by hand (see below).

flags.d: Always create a merge commit, even when a fast-forward is possible.
Cancel an in-progress merge and return to the pre-merge state.

Fast-forward

 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)

examples.desc: Show which files a merge would touch before doing it

gotchas: A conflict is not an error in git. It is git asking you to decide. `git merge --abort` always gets you back to safety.

blocks.name: git clone
blocks.sum: Copy an entire repository, history included, from a remote or a local path.

how.text: `git clone` creates a new folder, copies every commit and branch from the source, checks out the default branch and records the source as the remote named `origin`. The URL can be `https://...`, `git@host:user/repo.git` (SSH, see [Remote access with SSH](#ssh)) or a plain path on disk, which makes it easy to practice offline.

examples.desc: Clone a project from a remote
Clone every repository listed in a file

gotchas: Cloning over HTTPS to a private repository needs a token or credential helper; macOS stores credentials in the Keychain through `git-credential-osxkeychain`.

blocks.name: git remote
blocks.sum: Manage the named remote repositories your repository talks to.

how.text: A **remote** is a short name for another copy of the repository. The conventional name for the main one is `origin`. `git remote -v` lists the names with their fetch and push URLs. `git remote add origin URL` registers one. Nothing is transferred until you push, pull or fetch.

examples.desc: List remotes
Add a remote
Print just the push URL of origin

blocks.name: git push
blocks.sum: Upload your commits to a remote branch.

how.text: `git push` sends the commits the remote does not have and moves the remote branch pointer. The first time, `git push -u origin main` also records `origin/main` as the **upstream** of your `main`, so later a bare `git push` and `git pull` know where to go. The remote refuses a push that would discard commits it already has (a non-fast-forward); pull and merge first.

flags.d: Set the upstream branch for future pushes and pulls.

examples.desc: First push of main
examples.out:
To ../remote.git
 * [new branch]      main -> main
branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.

blocks.name: git pull
blocks.sum: Fetch new commits from the remote and merge them into the current branch.

how.text: `git pull` is `git fetch` (download the new commits and update `origin/main`) followed by a merge into your current branch. When your branch has not diverged, it is a fast-forward. With `--rebase` git replays your local commits on top of the fetched ones instead of creating a merge commit, giving a straight history. `git fetch` alone is safe: it updates `origin/*` and leaves your files alone.

flags.d: Replay local commits on top of the remote ones instead of merging.

blocks.name: git stash
blocks.sum: Put uncommitted changes on a shelf so you can switch tasks, then bring them back.
blocks.syntax: git stash [push -m message] | list | pop | apply | drop

how.text: `git stash push` saves your modified tracked files into a stack and restores a clean working tree. You can then switch branches or pull, and later `git stash pop` re-applies the most recent stash and removes it from the stack (`apply` keeps it). `git stash list` shows what is shelved. Untracked files are not stashed unless you add `-u`.

flags.d: Stash with a descriptive message.
Include untracked files.

examples.desc: Shelve work in progress and restore it
examples.code:
git stash push -m "half-done retry loop"
git stash list
git stash pop
examples.out: stash@{0}: On main: half-done retry loop

examples.desc: Delete every stash
examples.code:
git stash list | wc -l
git stash clear

gotchas: If `pop` hits a conflict, git keeps the stash so you do not lose it. Resolve, then `git stash drop`.

blocks.name: git restore
blocks.sum: Discard working-tree changes or unstage files.

how.text: `git restore file` overwrites the file in your working tree with the version in the staging area (or `HEAD`), discarding your edits permanently. `git restore --staged file` removes it from the staging area while leaving your edits in the file. `--source=HEAD~1 file` recovers the file as it was one commit ago.

flags.d: Unstage: undo a `git add`.
Take the file from the given commit.

examples.desc: Undo an accidental `git add`
Throw away your edits to a file

gotchas: Restoring working-tree changes cannot be undone: the edits were never committed, so git has no copy. Run `git diff` first if you are not sure.

blocks.text: .gitignore

blocks.name: .gitignore
blocks.sum: A file listing patterns of files git should not track.

how.text: Put a file named `.gitignore` at the top of the repository. Each line is a glob pattern: `*.log` ignores every log, `build/` ignores a directory, `!keep.log` makes an exception, and `#` starts a comment. Ignored files do not show in `git status` and are skipped by `git add`. Commit the `.gitignore` itself so everyone shares it. macOS adds `.DS_Store` files to every folder you open in Finder, so almost every Mac repository ignores them.

examples.desc: Ignore logs, macOS clutter and a virtual environment
See which files are being ignored right now

gotchas: Never commit passwords, API keys or private keys, even in a private repository. Once pushed they are in the history for good; rotate the secret.

blocks.text: Resolving a merge conflict

When two branches change the same line, git cannot decide, so it writes both versions into the file between markers and stops. Everything above `=======` is your branch (`HEAD`), everything below is the incoming branch.

blocks.code:
$ git merge timeout-5
Auto-merging check.zsh
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in check.zsh
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
$ git status -s
UU check.zsh
$ cat check.zsh
#!/bin/zsh
# check.zsh: report whether a host answers ping
host=${1:-example.com}
<<<<<<< HEAD
if ping -c 3 -t 1 "$host" > /dev/null 2>&1; then
=======
if ping -c 3 -t 5 "$host" > /dev/null 2>&1; then
>>>>>>> timeout-5
  echo "$host is up"
else
  echo "$host is down"
fi

blocks.text: The procedure is the same every time:

items.text: Open the file and decide what the final text should be. Keep one side, the other, or write a mix.
**Delete all three marker lines** (`<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`). A leftover marker is a syntax error in your script.
`git add check.zsh` to mark it resolved, then `git commit` (git pre-fills the merge message).
If it goes badly: `git merge --abort` returns you to before the merge.

blocks.text: `grep -rn '<<<<<<<' .` is a good last check that no markers remain.
Editors: nano and vim survival

You need a terminal text editor for `git commit` messages, config files and quick fixes over SSH. **nano** is the gentle one. **vim** is on every machine you will ever SSH into, so learn the escape route even if you never love it. (You will write most code in PyCharm; see [Setting up](#setup).)

blocks.name: nano
blocks.sum: A simple terminal text editor whose commands are listed at the bottom of the screen.

how.text: `nano file` opens the file (creating it when you save) and you type directly: there are no modes. The bottom two lines list the commands, where `^` means the Control key: `^O` is Control+O. After `^O` it asks for the file name; press Return to confirm. Since macOS 12.3 the `nano` command on a Mac is actually `pico`, the smaller editor nano was cloned from, so stick to the basics below, which are the same in both. `brew install nano` gives you a current one.

flags.d: Write Out: save the file.
Exit (asks to save if there are unsaved changes).
Cut the current line into the buffer.
Paste (uncut) the buffer.
Where is: search for text.
Show the built-in help.

examples.desc: Create and edit a script
Open at line 12
Edit every file that mentions a hostname (nano opens them one after another)

gotchas: Terminal.app sometimes sends Option-key combinations that nano does not understand. Stick to the Control shortcuts.

blocks.name: vim
blocks.sum: A modal text editor: keys do different things depending on the mode.

how.text: Vim has **modes**. You start in **normal mode**, where keys are commands (`dd` deletes a line), not text. Press `i` to enter **insert mode**, where typing inserts text; press `Esc` to return to normal mode. Press `:` in normal mode to type a command such as `:wq` at the bottom. Nearly every vim panic is "I typed and nothing happened" (you are in normal mode) or "I cannot get out". The cure for both is `Esc`, then a colon command.

flags.d: Enter insert mode before the cursor.
Leave insert mode, back to normal mode.
Write (save) the file.
Quit (fails if there are unsaved changes).
Save and quit (also `ZZ` in normal mode).
Quit and discard changes.
Delete the current line (and keep it in the register for `p`).
Undo.
Search forward; `n` jumps to the next match.

examples.desc: Open a file, add a line, save and quit
examples.code:
vim notes.txt
(press i, type text, press Esc, type :wq and Return)

examples.desc: Open the first file that matches a search

gotchas: A trapped terminal that does not respond to `:q` may be in insert mode: press `Esc` first. `⌃Z` suspends vim to the background; `fg` brings it back.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items.text: **Optimizing before measuring.** Make it correct, then measure (`time`, `timeit`), then fix the slowest part.
**Debugging by random edits.** Without a hypothesis you are just shuffling code. Reproduce first.
**Committing with `git add .` without looking.** Run `git status` and `git diff --staged` every time.
**Committing secrets or big binaries.** Use `.gitignore`; if a secret was pushed, rotate it.
**Giant commits with a message of "stuff".** One logical change per commit, a message that finishes the sentence "This commit will...".
**Leaving conflict markers in a file.** Search for `<<<<<<<` before committing a resolution.
**Treating `git restore file` as undoable.** It throws away uncommitted edits for good.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Trace the loop

task.text: Trace this program by hand with a table of `a`, `b` and `r`. What does it print, and how many times does the loop body run?

task.code:
a = 48
b = 18
while b != 0:
    r = a mod b
    a = b
    b = r
print a

hints: `48 mod 18` is the remainder of 48 divided by 18, which is 12.
Row by row: start (48, 18); after one pass (18, 12); keep going until `b` is 0.
blocks.solution:
pass 1: r = 12, a = 18, b = 12
pass 2: r = 6,  a = 12, b = 6
pass 3: r = 0,  a = 6,  b = 0
prints 6; the body ran 3 times

why.text: This is Euclid's algorithm for the greatest common divisor, and the same idea underlies reducing fractions. The table makes it trivial to see; guessing from the code would not.

blocks.title: Fix the host counter

task.text: `usable_hosts(prefix)` should return the number of usable host addresses in an IPv4 network with the given prefix length (from [Addressing & Subnetting](#addressing): a /24 gives 254). It has bugs. Reproduce each failing case, isolate it, and fix the function. Remember that a /31 has 2 usable addresses and a /32 has 1.

hints: Run `usable_hosts(24)` and compare with 254. How many bits are in the host part?
Host bits are `32 - prefix`. Then handle 31 and 32 before the general formula.

why.text: The first bug is the exponent: the number of addresses is 2 to the power of the **host** bits, not the prefix bits. The second is the edge cases, where subtracting 2 is wrong. Bugs sit at edges, so test the smallest and largest inputs.

blocks.check:
assert usable_hosts(24) == 254, "usable_hosts(24) should be 254"
assert usable_hosts(26) == 62, "usable_hosts(26) should be 62"
assert usable_hosts(30) == 2, "usable_hosts(30) should be 2"
assert usable_hosts(31) == 2, "a /31 has 2 usable addresses (point-to-point links)"
assert usable_hosts(32) == 1, "a /32 is a single host"
assert usable_hosts(8) == 16777214, "usable_hosts(8) should be 16777214"

blocks.title: Binary search

task.text: Write `find(items, target)` that returns the index of `target` in the sorted list `items`, or -1 if it is absent, using binary search. The check passes a list that counts how often you read from it and fails if you read more than 40 times in a list of a million.

hints: Keep two variables, `lo` and `hi`, for the part of the list that might still contain the target.
Loop while `lo <= hi`. Compare the middle item and move `lo` up or `hi` down by one.

why.text: The `lo <= hi` condition and the `+ 1` / `- 1` adjustments are where off-by-one bugs live. Testing the first item, the last item, a missing item and an empty list catches most of them.

blocks.check:
class CountingList(list):
    reads = 0
    def __getitem__(self, i):
        CountingList.reads += 1
        return super().__getitem__(i)
    def __iter__(self):
        raise AssertionError("do not loop over the list; use binary search")
data = CountingList(range(0, 2_000_000, 2))
CountingList.reads = 0
assert find(data, 1_000_000) == 500_000, "find(data, 1000000) should return 500000"
assert CountingList.reads <= 40, f"too many reads ({CountingList.reads}); halve the range each step"
assert find(data, 3) == -1, "3 is not in the list (only even numbers), expected -1"
assert find([], 5) == -1, "empty list returns -1"
assert find([5], 5) == 0, "single item"
assert find([1, 3, 5, 7], 7) == 3, "last item"
assert find([1, 3, 5, 7], 1) == 0, "first item"

blocks.title: Plan before you code

task.text: Write pseudocode (plain English, indented) for a script that watches your router: ping it once every 10 seconds, and print a message with the time when the router stops answering and another when it comes back. Then list the sub-steps you would test first.

hints: You need one piece of remembered state: was the router up at the last check?
blocks.solution:
set was_up to true
repeat forever:
    ping the router once with a 2 second timeout
    if the ping got a reply:
        if was_up is false: print the time and "router is back"
        set was_up to true
    else:
        if was_up is true: print the time and "router is down"
        set was_up to false
    wait 10 seconds
test first: a single ping command, then its exit status, then the if/else on one host, then the loop

why.text: The variable `was_up` makes the difference between printing on every failure and printing only on **changes**. State between iterations is what turns a loop into a monitor, and you build exactly this in [Reachability and path](#net-reach).

blocks.title: Fix the broken pipeline

task.text: In `~/lab`, this pipeline is meant to show the three most common HTTP status codes in `access.log`. It prints a long list with many repeated counts instead. Reproduce it, work out which stage is wrong, and fix it.

hints: Cut the pipeline after `uniq -c` and look at the output. Are identical codes next to each other?
blocks.solution: awk '{print $9}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3

why.text: Without `sort` the same status code appears in many separate runs, and `uniq -c` counts each run separately. You found it by the isolate step: run the first two stages alone and look.

blocks.title: A git workflow with a deliberate conflict

task.text: In a new folder `~/lab/conflict`, create a repository with one file `greeting.txt` containing `hello`, and commit it on `main`. Create a branch `loud` that changes the line to `HELLO` and commit. Switch back to `main`, change the same line to `hello world` and commit. Merge `loud` into `main`, which will conflict. Resolve it so the file contains `HELLO WORLD`, finish the merge, and show the history as a graph.

hints: `git switch -c loud`, edit, `git commit -am "shout"`, `git switch main`, edit the same line, commit, then `git merge loud`.
Open `greeting.txt`, replace the whole conflict block (including the three marker lines) with the line you want, then `git add greeting.txt && git commit`.
blocks.solution:
mkdir -p ~/lab/conflict && cd ~/lab/conflict && git init -b main
echo hello > greeting.txt && git add greeting.txt && git commit -m "Add greeting"
git switch -c loud
echo HELLO > greeting.txt && git commit -am "Shout"
git switch main
echo "hello world" > greeting.txt && git commit -am "Add world"
git merge loud
echo "HELLO WORLD" > greeting.txt
git add greeting.txt && git commit -m "Merge loud"
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all

why.text: Both branches changed the same line after the split, so git could not choose. Resolving means writing the final content, removing the markers, staging and committing. The graph then shows a merge commit with two parents.

questions.q: Why must a list be sorted before binary search?

options.text: Binary search reads items from the end
Each comparison with the middle item discards half the list only if order tells you which half
Binary search only works on numbers

questions.why: If the list is in random order, "the target is smaller than the middle item" tells you nothing about which side to keep.

questions.q: A loop inside another loop, both over the same n-item list, has which complexity?
questions.why: For each of the n outer items the inner loop does n steps, so about n times n operations.

questions.q: Which structure is the best fit for "have I seen this IP before?" over a million log lines?

options.text: A list, scanning from the start each time

questions.why: A set answers membership tests in roughly constant time. A list needs a scan of up to a million items for every line.

questions.q: In a Python traceback, where is the most useful line?

options.text: The last line, giving the exception type and message

questions.why: The bottom shows what went wrong; the lines above show the path of calls that led there.

questions.q: Which command undoes a `git add` but keeps your edits in the file?
questions.why: `git restore --staged {{file}}` removes the file from the staging area only. Plain `git restore file` would discard the edits.

options.text: Uploads local commits to the remote
Shows the difference with the remote
Fetches new commits from the remote and merges them into the current branch

questions.why: `git pull` is `git fetch` followed by a merge (or a rebase with `--rebase`).

blocks.text: You will version a tiny script from scratch and practice the entire everyday git loop against a "remote" that is only a folder on your disk, so nothing needs a network or an account. The same commands work unchanged against GitHub later.
Step 1: Create the repo and the first commit

blocks.code:
mkdir -p ~/lab/hello-repo && cd ~/lab/hello-repo
git init -b main

blocks.text: Create the script (in PyCharm, or with `nano check.zsh`):

blocks.code:
#!/bin/zsh
# check.zsh: report whether a host answers ping
host=${1:-example.com}
if ping -c 1 -t 2 "$host" > /dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "$host is up"
else
  echo "$host is down"
fi

chmod +x check.zsh
git status
git add check.zsh
git commit -m "Add check.zsh"
git log --oneline

blocks.text: Step 2: Ignore what does not belong

blocks.code:
printf '*.log\n.DS_Store\n' > .gitignore
touch debug.log
git status -s

blocks.text: You should see only `?? .gitignore`: `debug.log` is ignored. Commit the ignore file: `git add .gitignore && git commit -m "Ignore logs"`.
Step 3: Change on a branch, then merge

blocks.code:
git switch -c feature/retries
sed -i '' 's/-c 1/-c 3/' check.zsh
git diff
git commit -am "Send three probes"
git switch main
git merge feature/retries
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all

blocks.text: Because `main` did not move while the branch existed, git fast-forwards. The graph is a single line. Repeat with a change on both branches and use `git merge --no-ff` to see a real merge commit.
Step 4: Add a remote, push, clone and pull

blocks.code:
git init --bare ~/lab/remote.git
git remote add origin ~/lab/remote.git
git push -u origin main
git clone ~/lab/remote.git ~/lab/copy
cd ~/lab/copy && echo "# notes" > NOTES.md
git add NOTES.md && git commit -m "Add notes" && git push
cd ~/lab/hello-repo && git pull
git log --oneline

blocks.text: You now have two working copies and a shared repository, and have moved a commit between them in both directions.
Step 5: Break it and recover

Edit `check.zsh` badly, run `git diff`, then recover with `git restore check.zsh`. Make a commit you regret and undo it by keeping the work but un-committing: `git reset --soft HEAD~1`, which moves the branch back one commit and leaves the changes staged.

Add `git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --decorate --all"` and use `git lg`. Put `check.zsh` into `~/bin` by symlink so it is on your `PATH`; you will learn how in [Scripting](#scripting).
Next: [Your first zsh session](#zsh-basics) starts the shell part of the book: how the shell reads a command line, finds programs and expands what you type.

terms.def: A precise, step-by-step procedure for solving a kind of problem
A plan written in plain English with the shape of code: sequence, decisions and loops
A notation describing how an algorithm's cost grows with input size, such as O(n) or O(log n)
Finding an item in a sorted list by repeatedly halving the range to examine
A way of organizing data so particular operations (lookup, ordering, traversal) are cheap
A dictionary: a structure mapping keys to values with near-constant-time lookup
Python's report of the chain of calls leading to an error, with the error message on the last line
A folder under version control, holding your files and their full history in a hidden .git directory
A saved snapshot of the staged files with a message, author and pointer to its parent
A movable label pointing at a commit, used to develop changes in parallel
A state where two branches changed the same lines and git needs you to choose the result
A named copy of the repository elsewhere, conventionally called origin
The set of changes selected with git add that the next commit will contain
An editor, like vim, in which the same key does different things depending on the current mode
